turns.question: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: hardest bug, first suspicion, what proved it
card.say: The hardest bug was a plan that came back with a product ID we couldn't book. It only happened with a few destinations, so I couldn't reproduce it at first. I first suspected the model was picking products that were sold out. The logs showed the model was fine. The real cause was our product tool returning an old ID after a product was replaced. I replayed the saved request and response, and the same wrong ID came back every time.
card.then: Next: the fix, and how I stopped it from coming back.

more: The product tool was returning an old product ID that had been replaced, so it was no longer bookable. I replayed the saved request and response, and it happened every time. The fix was to check every returned ID against the current catalog before we showed the plan, and we also added a fallback so that if a stale ID slips through, the plan shows the nearest available alternative instead of failing.

turns.name: W2-dyn
turns.question: You said the repository saves the intent with its client ID before the request goes out — on Android, what exactly gets written to local storage at that moment, and how does the app use it after a crash mid-send?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures
card.adopted: MVP path: send money to a contact, with balance and history; server ledger is the single source of truth, phone keeps a local copy for display and offline reading only
card.constraints: ["Start by clarifying the requirements; define the MVP user path"]
card.heard: what gets written to local storage and how the app uses it after a crash
card.say: At that moment the repository writes one row: the client transfer ID, the payer, the recipient, 8000 cents, and a status of pending. It writes the row before the request goes out, so the row exists even if the app dies. After a crash, the app reads that row and shows "processing", not "failed". Then it asks the server for that same ID and shows whatever the server says. If the lookup finds nothing, the state stays unknown, because the request may still be in flight.
card.then: Next: the server's idempotency contract for a resend of that same ID.

more: The row also keeps a timestamp and a retry count, so the app knows how old the intent is. On restart, the app reads any row still marked pending. It shows "processing" and asks the server for that same client ID. It never sends a new ID, because the server treats a repeat of the same ID as the same transfer. If the server says it's done, the row becomes success.

turns.question: Your sequence ends with "S-->>R: Transfer record" and "R-->>A: Result screen: success," which assumes the response arrives. If the server commits but the response is lost and Android kills the process, what does A see on reopen, and what does the repository do with that pending row? Please update your sequence diagram.

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures
card.adopted: MVP path: send money to a contact, with balance and history; server ledger is the single source of truth, phone keeps a local copy for display and offline reading only
card.constraints: ["Start by clarifying the requirements; define the MVP user path"]
card.heard: response lost, process killed, what does the app and repository do with the pending row
card.say: On reopen, the app reads the pending row from the database and shows "processing", not "failed". The repository then asks the server for that same client transfer ID. It never sends a new ID, because the server treats a repeat of the same ID as the same transfer. If the server says it's done, the row becomes success, and the result screen reads only from the database. I'd resend that same client ID only while the server's idempotency window still covers it; after that, I'd rely on the lookup and reconciliation, never a new ID. The server answers a repeat of that ID with the original transfer's status, so the ledger still has only one transfer.

more: The row also keeps a timestamp and a retry count, so the app knows how old the intent is. On restart it reads every row still marked pending, not only the last one. If two sends were in flight, each one gets its own lookup by its own client ID. The server answers a repeat of that ID with the original transfer's status, so the ledger still has only one transfer.

turns.name: W3-dyn
turns.question: You said you'd resend the same client ID only while the idempotency window still covers it — so what does the user see if that window has already expired by the time the app reopens and does its lookup?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures
card.adopted: MVP path: send money to a contact, with balance and history; server ledger is the single source of truth, phone keeps a local copy for display and offline reading only
card.constraints: ["Start by clarifying the requirements; define the MVP user path"]
card.heard: idempotency window already expired when the app reopens
card.say: Right, so the window has passed and we can't resend. The row stays "processing" and the app only does the lookup. If the lookup still finds nothing, the state stays unknown, not failed. The user sees "still checking" with the amount and recipient, and a note that we'll update it. I'd also show a support path, so they can ask us to check the ledger by hand.

Today we'll start with a project you really owned, then design a fictional mobile wallet together. I'll add a few new conditions along the way, and leave time for your questions at the end.
Interviewer: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?
Candidate: The project I owned most was the AI trip planner at KKday.
Candidate: I was the technical lead for a team of five.
Candidate: Travelers used it in the KKday app, on Google Play, in many markets.
Candidate: Planning a trip by hand was slow.
Candidate: You work out the budget, search products one by one, then put the plan together.
Candidate: The planner took a destination, a budget and a number of days, and built a plan the user could book.
Candidate: My responsibility started at the technical plan and the agent design, and ended at the core backend and the Android code that reads the streamed plan.
Candidate: I didn't own the product decisions or the app screens outside the planner.

Interviewer: You said your responsibility ended at the core backend and the Android code that reads the streamed plan on the AI trip planner at KKday. Within that, which exact pieces did you build yourself versus what your team of five built?
Candidate: I built the agent design and the core backend myself.
Candidate: I also wrote the Android code that reads the streamed plan.
Candidate: The other four people built the app screens around the planner, the product and order tools, and the personalization data.
Candidate: I set the response format with the app team, but I didn't build those screens.
Candidate: I also owned the checks on each plan, the retry with the exact error, and the safe fallback.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: I'll take the follow-up question "change a stop" in the trip plan.
Candidate: The user taps a stop and picks a new one.
Candidate: The app sends the change to the backend with the saved plan progress.
Candidate: The backend asks the agent for a new plan, then checks the structure, product IDs and location limits.
Candidate: If a check fails, it retries with the exact error.
Candidate: After the retry limit, it falls back to a safe default, so the user never gets a broken plan.
Interviewer: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?
Candidate: The hardest bug was a plan that came back with a product ID we couldn't book.
Candidate: It only happened with a few destinations, so I couldn't reproduce it at first.
Candidate: I first suspected the model was picking products that were sold out.
Candidate: The logs showed the model was fine.
Candidate: The real cause was our product tool returning an old ID after a product was replaced.
Candidate: I replayed the saved request and response, and the same wrong ID came back every time.
Candidate: The product tool was returning an old product ID that had been replaced, so it was no longer bookable.
Candidate: I replayed the saved request and response, and it happened every time.

Candidate: The fix was to check every returned ID against the current catalog before we showed the plan, and we also added a fallback so that if a stale ID slips through, the plan shows the nearest available alternative instead of failing.
Interviewer: You said you replayed the saved request and response and the same wrong ID came back every time — how did that prove the product tool was the source rather than your own catalog lookup?
Candidate: The replay showed the wrong ID came back from the product tool itself.
Candidate: My own lookup only read what the tool returned, so it couldn't have made that ID.
Candidate: When I called the tool directly with the same request, it gave the same old ID.
Candidate: That proved the source was the tool, not my code.
Interviewer: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?
Candidate: There were two other options.
Candidate: First, I could filter the IDs only in my own lookup.
Candidate: Second, I could ask the product tool team to fix it and wait.
Candidate: I didn't pick the first one, because my lookup only reads what the tool returns, so the bad ID would still come back.
Candidate: I didn't pick the second one alone, because the fix would take time and users were still getting broken plans.
Candidate: So I added the catalog check as a guard, and raised the tool bug with its owners.
Candidate: After release, I checked it with our tests and the logs from real users; they only cover the cases we saw, so they can't prove there's no problem on devices or networks we didn't test.
Candidate: After release, I watched the logs for plans that hit the fallback, and that number went down.
Candidate: I also checked that no plan with a stale ID reached users in the cases we could see.
Candidate: The limit is that this only covers the cases we saw; it can't prove there's no problem on devices or networks we didn't test.

Interviewer: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?
Candidate: At Debon Securities, I was moving part of our trading app to the new navigation.

Candidate: I finished the fix and the testing myself, and my change shipped in the next release.
Candidate: If he had refused to delay, I'd have explained the risk clearly: which pages could break, and for how many users.
